questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((-x)^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{4}\frac{7{x}^{3}}{1+2{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\sqrt[3]{-x} \\  & =-\sqrt[3]{x} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x)=\frac{7{x}^{3}}{1+2{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}h(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{-e}^{0}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x=A,$ what is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{e}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =({e}^{-x}-{e}^{-(-x)}) \\  & =({e}^{-x}-{e}^{x}) \\  & =-({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-e}^{e}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-e}^{e}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-e}^{0}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{e}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ A+{\int }_{0}^{e}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{0}^{e}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .
$$

Notice that $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function, we have

$$
\int_{-2}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.
$$

\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =4(-x)^{3} \\  & =-4{x}^{3} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
\int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

- The function $g(x) = e^x+e^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & ={e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & ={e}^{-x}+{e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}+{e}^{-x} \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x) = \sin(2x)$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form $\displaystyle \int_{-a}^a h(x)\,\textrm d x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. So, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,$ what is the value of $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x  \, \textrm dx?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Notice that $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
\int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x  \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$
